rows.evidence: Q1: Chapter 4 'Sensitivity analysis of the ELIDM' (Fig. 45) reports the authors' own model runs of network cost versus number of randomly generated flow regimes for a real Italian network; Annex 1 reports the authors' own calibration of the Clement model using discharges recorded by a Venturi meter at the head of District 4 of the Sinistra Ofanto scheme (Tables A3, A4); Chapter 5 Applications 1-4 report model runs on real networks (582 ha and 1340 ha schemes).
rows.notes: The paper is an FAO design/analysis manual (I&D Paper 59) that also contains original applications, so Q1 is answered yes with some doubt. It does not, however, report any result of its own comparing the investment cost of on-demand networks with that of rotation or other delivery schedules, nor does it attribute a higher cost to guaranteeing peak-period supply. What it shows is related preconditions: the design discharge of an on-demand network must exceed the continuous (24 h) flow by 27-98% depending on r and hydrant elasticity (Fig. 10, Chapter 3), and network cost rises and then stabilises as more flow regimes are included in the ELIDM optimisation (Fig. 45); Chapter 6 states qualitatively that pipe extension to very small holdings is expensive and that O&M charges are somewhat higher than in open-canal systems, without own data. These support a mechanism but not the claimed cost comparison, so Q2 is no and upstream is set true.

notes: Full text appears complete (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 59, Lamaddalena & Sagardoy 2000, including Annexes 1-3). The publication is primarily a methodological guideline with an accompanying software package (COPAM); original results are limited to model applications on Italian networks, a sensitivity analysis of optimisation cost versus number of flow regimes, and a field calibration of the Clement formula.
